result:
The cursor blinks like a metronome, steady and impatient. It keeps time with everything that isn't yet said—the sentences that might be beautiful, the ones that would make a laugh, the ones that would scar. I sit and watch it for a while, as though blinking back might coax something out of the white. Whatever comes to me arrives in fragments at first: a smell of rain on hot asphalt, a child's crumpled drawing, the memory of a laugh that used to belong to someone I loved.

There's a certain generosity to nothing in particular. When you give yourself permission to be aimless, the mind becomes a crowded waiting room where strangers in different outfits take turns telling you their small stories. A woman in a yellow raincoat unrolls a map that has no names. A man with tape on his glasses recites a poem he learned at age seven. An old dog sighs and shows me a scar behind its ear. I take notes. Some details are stickier than others—the map, the dog—so I fold them into my pocket.

Outside, the city hums like a refrigerator, steady and indifferent. People move with the passion of errands: bread, bus passes, apologies delivered to voicemail. Once, on the bus, an old man held a photograph so close his eyes were in it. He tapped the glass with the kind of reverence I usually reserve for sunsets. I wanted to ask about the person in the picture, but instead he slipped the photo into a book and closed it like a secret. That small refusal stayed with me. There are thousands of private landscapes nested like Russian dolls inside public bodies. We protect them with thin, pragmatic lids.

I think, sometimes, of the ways we fixate on endpoints: the neat bow of a delivered verdict, the final period after a long story. But most of life is commas, suspended and leaning into what comes next. The commas are noisy. They carry laundry, groceries, furtive kisses in stairwells, unpaid parking tickets. They also carry music—the kind that wells up after something breaks and you realize you're still alive. When you pay attention, the interim is crowded with beauty better than any resolution: the way a stray cat will walk across a piano bench as if it owns Bach; the sound of words misread and then corrected, a small laughter in the throat.

A friend once told me she collects names the way some people collect stamps. Not the names of famous people or lost lovers—just names that feel like good tools. "Ester," she said, listing it like a new spoon. "Bram," she added, like a reliable compass. It occurred to me that names are a sort of currency; they can buy you an identity for the afternoon. If I were to be honest, I'd say I hoard phrases: "for what it's worth," "if you can," "remember to breathe." They live in a jar on the shelf of my sentences, and sometimes, when the night tilts toward a certain kind of loneliness, I open the jar and let a phrase fall into my lap. It makes a sound like a coin.

There is an odd thrill in discovering that a small, everyday thing is also a metaphor. A mug of tea becomes an orbit. A subway station becomes a cathedral. But metaphors are shy; if you push them too hard, they fake sincerity and collapse into clichés. Better to let them show you themselves, like the way light will find the crack in your apartment floor and announce that the day is young. I prefer, these days, images that arrive quietly. A leaf drifting past the library window and pausing on the sill as if it had come this far just to witness somebody reading—this feels truer than any grand statement about the human condition.

There are recipes in the small acts, too. When grief comes—because it will, like a thunderstorm—there is an art to folding it into ordinary life. You can learn to make a proper stew out of loneliness: toss in a bay leaf of memory, a cup of stubbornness, a tablespoon of ritual. Simmer. Eat with friends who do not ask questions they don't mean. Oftentimes, the dish tastes better than the feeling that birthed it. The point is not to eliminate the bruise but to cook with it.

I am aware, in a not-very-practical way, of how much of my interior life is a rehearsal for some future letter I will never write. I practice empathy on strangers who might not exist tomorrow. I craft apologies I will never need to deliver. Perhaps this is a form of exercise, like warming up before a run, or perhaps it's a species-level nervous habit—preparing speeches for a play that is still being cast. Either way, the preparation is useful. It teaches you, in low stakes, how to survive the real ones.

Tonight, I will finish this thing and then get up and make coffee. I'll stand at the window, cup in both hands, and watch the sky try on different blues. There will be a dog barking two blocks away and someone playing a wrong note on a piano that is nonetheless trying, valiantly, to be a song. I will think of the people who are kind to strangers, of the people who are not, of the tiny bright wells of courage people carry like coins to drop into stranger machines. Courage is not always big. Sometimes it's small and private: leaving a note on a neighbor's door when you notice their plant is dying, calling your mother back, opening the door when you don't want to.

If you asked me what this piece is about, I could offer a reasonable answer framed in tidy language: it's about attention, about the generous clutter of everyday life, about the commas. But there's a simpler truth: I wrote because the cursor blinked and something wanted to move. The sentences came like people at a party who didn't know each other but liked the music. Some will stay, some will leave. I will fold the rest into my pockets and keep walking.

So take whatever comes to you—names, rain, the wrong song that gets stuck in your head—and treat it as a gift, even when it's small or bruised. Open the jar on your shelf and let a phrase drop out. Make your stew. Watch the light find the crack. The world keeps offering tiny, persistent miracles; all you need is the ability to see them between the blinks.
